article.title: Lockheed Martin Guarantees $500 Million Loan to ULA as Vulcan Grounding Drains Space Segment Profit
article.summary: Lockheed Martin disclosed a $500 million loan guarantee for United Launch Alliance and cut its space division's profit forecast after Vulcan's grounding.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

United Launch Alliance's corporate parents have guaranteed a loan to the company as it addresses "financial challenges" caused by the grounding of its Vulcan Centaur rocket, according to [SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/ula-deals-with-financial-challenges-caused-by-vulcan-grounding/). In a Securities and Exchange Commission filing tied to its second-quarter results on July 23, Lockheed Martin disclosed that it provided a bank guarantee for a loan taken by ULA during the quarter, [SpaceNews reported](https://spacenews.com/ula-deals-with-financial-challenges-caused-by-vulcan-grounding/).

## What We Know

Lockheed's filing states that "in the second quarter of 2026, we agreed to guarantee certain ULA borrowings under which maximum potential future payments amount to $500 million," according to [SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/ula-deals-with-financial-challenges-caused-by-vulcan-grounding/), which reviewed the filing. Lockheed recognized the fair value of that guarantee obligation at $64 million in the second quarter, per the same filing cited by [SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/ula-deals-with-financial-challenges-caused-by-vulcan-grounding/).

The guarantee coincided with a cut to Lockheed's financial outlook for its space division: the company reduced its profit forecast for the segment from a range of $1.385 billion to $1.415 billion down to between $1.34 billion and $1.38 billion, [SpaceNews reported](https://spacenews.com/ula-deals-with-financial-challenges-caused-by-vulcan-grounding/). Lockheed's own [second-quarter earnings release](https://news.lockheedmartin.com/2026-07-23-Lockheed-Martin-Reports-Second-Quarter-2026-Financial-Results) shows the Space segment posted $3,496 million in revenue and $371 million in operating profit for the quarter, an operating margin of 10.6%, compared with $3,307 million in revenue and $362 million in operating profit a year earlier.

Lockheed's filing also flags a broader, forward-looking commitment: among its listed risk factors, the company references joint ventures "including United Launch Alliance, for which the company has provided and expects to provide additional financial guarantees," according to [Lockheed Martin's own earnings release](https://news.lockheedmartin.com/2026-07-23-Lockheed-Martin-Reports-Second-Quarter-2026-Financial-Results). In its SEC filing, Lockheed stated that "we and Boeing expect to provide additional financial support to ULA to support its liquidity or ongoing operations and could incur impairment and operating losses if the Vulcan Centaur rocket does not perform consistent with ULA's assumptions," [SpaceNews reported](https://spacenews.com/ula-deals-with-financial-challenges-caused-by-vulcan-grounding/). ULA is jointly owned by Lockheed Martin and Boeing. [SpaceNews noted](https://spacenews.com/ula-deals-with-financial-challenges-caused-by-vulcan-grounding/) that neither Lockheed nor ULA said whether Boeing also participated in the specific $500 million guarantee disclosed this quarter.

The financial strain traces back to a solid rocket booster problem that has kept Vulcan grounded since February. Lockheed's "performance challenges" language refers to an anomaly with one of the solid rocket boosters on a Vulcan launch that month, [SpaceNews reported](https://spacenews.com/ula-deals-with-financial-challenges-caused-by-vulcan-grounding/). The vehicle still completed its mission, delivering a payload for the U.S. Space Force designated USSF-87, but Vulcan has not flown since, according to the same report. A similar anomaly had already occurred on Vulcan's second launch, in October 2024, [SpaceNews noted](https://spacenews.com/ula-deals-with-financial-challenges-caused-by-vulcan-grounding/).

In a statement carried by [SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/ula-deals-with-financial-challenges-caused-by-vulcan-grounding/), ULA said that "ULA's financial position has been impacted due to the performance challenges associated with the anomaly with the solid rocket booster nozzle experienced on two of the Vulcan launches." The company added: "While this is a challenging time bringing our Vulcan rocket up to its optimal launch rate, ULA is well positioned for the future and continues to be laser focused on our customers' needs and achieving a reliable and sustainable manifest."

The gap between ULA's ambitions and its actual launch cadence this year is stark. At a briefing in February, two days before the USSF-87 launch, the company said it expected to perform 18 to 22 launches in 2026, including four Atlas 5 launches and up to 18 Vulcan launches, [SpaceNews reported](https://spacenews.com/ula-deals-with-financial-challenges-caused-by-vulcan-grounding/). Vulcan has not launched again since USSF-87, per the same report.

Northrop Grumman, which supplies the solid rocket booster motors, addressed the fix during its own July 21 earnings call, saying it had redesigned components on the motor that have since been confirmed in a static-fire test, but cautioned that it may not begin delivering the redesigned motors until the end of the year, [SpaceNews reported](https://spacenews.com/ula-deals-with-financial-challenges-caused-by-vulcan-grounding/).

## What We Don't Know

Neither Lockheed nor ULA has said whether Boeing separately guaranteed any portion of the $500 million in ULA borrowings, [per SpaceNews](https://spacenews.com/ula-deals-with-financial-challenges-caused-by-vulcan-grounding/). Neither company has specified exactly when Vulcan will return to flight, and Northrop Grumman's own timeline for delivering redesigned booster motors extends only to "the end of the year," leaving the return-to-flight date for Vulcan's next mission unclear.

## Context

The disclosure follows [The Machine Herald's prior coverage](/article/2026-05/16-ula-confirms-successful-gem-63xl-static-fire-as-vulcan-srb-investigation-drags-on-and-space-force-pause-holds) of the solid rocket booster investigation and the U.S. Space Force's pause on Vulcan missions, and comes the same week NASA [reassigned its SunRISE solar-storm mission](/article/2026-07/24-nasa-reassigns-sunrise-solar-storm-mission-from-ulas-vulcan-centaur-to-spacex-falcon-heavy) from Vulcan Centaur to a SpaceX Falcon Heavy. The loan guarantee marks the clearest sign yet that the months-long grounding has moved beyond a technical and scheduling problem into measurable financial exposure for both of ULA's parent companies.
